name: Denise Kavanagh
presenting_complaint: Collapse at home, found hypotensive and clammy, cause unclear

medical_history.social: Lives alone, independent. Non-smoker. Rare alcohol.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 68-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance after collapsing at home. She is confused, pale, cool and clammy with a thready pulse. The cause of her hypotension is not yet clear. Background: type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and atrial fibrillation on apixaban. Obs: BP 78/44, HR 128, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air, temp 37.4, GCS 14.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Collateral/history to categorise shock: preceding chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, fever, bleeding (including GI/PR — she is anticoagulated), vomiting/diarrhoea, allergen exposure
Explicitly note anticoagulation (apixaban) and beta-blockade (metoprolol may blunt tachycardic response) from the drug history
Fluid losses, oral intake, recent illness/infection symptoms, and any trauma or falls
Document allergies (penicillin) and full medication list; establish time of onset and last known well
objective: A-to-E assessment; insert TWO large-bore IV cannulas and take bloods at cannulation
Bloods including VBG with LACTATE (marker of hypoperfusion), FBC, UEC, LFT, coags, troponin, blood cultures, group and hold/crossmatch
Bedside tests: 12-lead ECG (ischaemia/arrhythmia), BGL, pregnancy test if applicable, and POCUS if credentialed (heart/IVC/lungs/aorta/FAST)
Insert URINARY CATHETER for hourly output as a real-time perfusion marker
Focused exam for the shock categories: JVP, heart sounds/murmurs, chest auscultation, tracheal position, abdomen/aorta, calves, skin (rash/urticaria), PR for melaena
assessment: Undifferentiated shock with organ hypoperfusion — work systematically through the FOUR categories rather than a random differential list
Hypovolaemic: haemorrhage (GI bleed on apixaban, ruptured AAA), dehydration
Cardiogenic: MI, arrhythmia, valve failure (relevant given IHD/AF); Obstructive: PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax
plan: A-to-E, two large-bore cannulas, bloods with VBG and lactate, fluid challenge, cardiac monitor, and urinary catheter for output (FIRST actions)
Give a fluid challenge (e.g. 250-500 mL balanced crystalloid bolus, up to ~30 mL/kg) and reassess response

Systematically exclude each category OUT LOUD: hypovolaemic (bleeding/dehydration), distributive (sepsis/anaphylaxis/neurogenic), cardiogenic (infarct/arrhythmia/valve), obstructive (PE/tamponade/tension pneumothorax)

Empirical treatment while investigating: if sepsis suspected, take cultures and give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour (use non-penicillin agent given allergy); if anaphylaxis, IM adrenaline; if arrhythmia, treat per ALS
Send lactate and repeat to track resuscitation; assess for occult haemorrhage given anticoagulation and consider reversal if bleeding source found
If still hypotensive after ~30 mL/kg fluid: commence vasopressors (e.g. noradrenaline) and refer ICU; escalate to ED consultant early
Serial reassessment of obs, GCS, lactate and urine output; disposition to ICU/HDU

critical_errors: Failing to work through ALL FOUR shock categories (hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive) and instead reeling off a random differential list, causing a treatable cause (e.g. tamponade, tension pneumothorax, occult haemorrhage) to be missed
Omitting VBG/lactate and a urinary catheter, leaving no objective marker of perfusion to guide resuscitation
Not recognising occult haemorrhage in an anticoagulated (apixaban) patient whose beta-blocker may mask the expected tachycardic response
must_not_miss: Obstructive shock (PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax) actively considered and excluded
Sepsis with time-critical antibiotics and cultures if distributive shock suspected
Occult haemorrhage on anticoagulation as a hypovolaemic cause
